# Acquiring maps {#acquisition}

Every analysis starts with a study area and a maps object. There are four routes
to it: selective download of MapBiomas tiles, the national collection stored on
your computer, selective reading over HTTP, and a local folder with maps of any
collection. All of them lead to the same object, used by every other function in
the package.

## Study area {-}

The area is a polygon in any coordinate reference system, stored as a
GeoPackage (`.gpkg`), shapefile (`.shp`, with its `.prj`) or GeoJSON, or already
loaded as an `sf` object. The path can be given with or without extension, or be
the folder holding a single area file; with `.gpkg` and `.shp` of the same name,
the `.gpkg` is used. The package already includes the boundary of the UFSCar
Lagoa do Sino campus, used in this chapter:

```{r}
ufscar <- system.file("shp", "UFSCar.shp", package = "biomastats")
```

::: {.atencao}
A shapefile is a set of files. Without its `.prj`, it loses its coordinate
reference system and loading stops with a message. When copying or sending an
area, include every file of the same name, or prefer a GeoPackage, which is a
single file.
:::

When no area is at hand, `make_polygon()` draws the area from a centre
point, a shape (`"circle"`, `"square"` or `"hexagon"`) and the total width in km
(`size`), which is the circle's diameter, the square's side or the distance
between opposite vertices of the hexagon. A hexagon of about 12.5 km² centred on
the campus, like the example area in Part II, looks like this:

```{r eval=FALSE}
area <- make_polygon(lat = -23.605, lon = -48.529, size = 4.4,
                     shape = "hexagon")
```

::: {.atencao}
`make_polygon()` writes the result as `polygon.shp` in the `shp` folder of the
installed package, replacing the previous file. To keep an area, save the
returned object (`area$polygon`) with `sf::st_write()` in a folder of your own.
:::

MapBiomas splits Brazil into tiles, and `compare_shapefiles()` tells you which
ones cover the area. Lagoa do Sino fits entirely within tile 93:

```{r}
unique(compare_shapefiles(ufscar))
```

```{r tile-grid, echo=FALSE, fig.height=5.5, out.width="80%", fig.cap="Tile grid used for selective acquisition. Highlighted: tile 93, which contains Lagoa do Sino (dot)."}
grade <- sf::st_read(system.file("shp", "brasil_cortado.shp", package = "biomastats"), quiet = TRUE)
grade$id <- seq_len(nrow(grade))
grade$usado <- grade$id %in% compare_shapefiles(ufscar)
ponto <- sf::st_centroid(sf::st_union(sf::st_transform(sf::st_read(ufscar, quiet = TRUE), sf::st_crs(grade))))
ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_sf(data = grade, ggplot2::aes(fill = usado), colour = "#c9c1ad", linewidth = .25) +
  ggplot2::geom_sf(data = ponto, colour = "#22302a", size = 2.2) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#f3ecdc", `TRUE` = "#3b7d3a"), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::theme_void()
```

## Route 1: selective download {-}

Here the package downloads from the Bioma Stats API only the tiles and years
the area needs. If the area crosses more than one tile, the neighbouring tiles
are merged before the final crop and the mask by the boundary. The files are
kept in the folder you choose and reused in later runs.

```{r eval=FALSE}
maps <- load_rasters(ufscar, start = 1985, end = 2024, method = "download",
                     export_folder_path = "mapbiomas-tiles")
```

## Route 2: local national collection {-}

Here the national map for each year is downloaded only once. After that, any
area can be cropped from it without an internet connection, which makes this
route the better choice for many areas or for large ones.

```{r eval=FALSE}
download_mapbiomas(dest_dir = "collection_10", data_type = "cover",
                   collection = 10, time_range = c(1985, 2024))

maps <- load_rasters(ufscar, start = 1985, end = 2024, method = "library",
                     import_folder_path = "collection_10")
```

::: {.nota}
Both routes produce the same object: for the Lagoa do Sino example area, the 40
maps cropped from the national collection are identical, cell by cell, to those
obtained by selective download.
:::

## Route 3: selective reading over HTTP {-}

MapBiomas annual maps are in a public repository, as GeoTIFFs split into blocks.
With `method = "http"`, `load_rasters()` reads only the blocks that cover the
area, without login and without downloading the whole national file. The
catalogue lists the available collections, for Brazil (30 m and 10 m) and other
countries and regions:

```{r}
catalogue <- raster_catalog()
columns <- c(Product = "id", `Resolution (m)` = "resolution_m",
             `First year` = "first_year", `Last year` = "last_year")
tabela(stats::setNames(catalogue[, columns], names(columns)), 0)
```

The product is chosen by its `id`. With `export_folder_path`, the windows read
are saved as `product_year.tif`, together with the area (`area.gpkg`):

```{r eval=FALSE}
maps_http <- load_rasters(ufscar, start = 2023, end = 2024, method = "http",
                          product = "mapbiomas_brasil_c10",
                          export_folder_path = "maps-lagoa")
```

Any other annual GeoTIFF split into blocks can be read too, with `url` and
`{year}` in place of the year. Brazilian collections use the MapBiomas legend;
those of other countries have their own legends, which come in through the
dictionary (next section).

## Route 4: local folder, any collection {-}

Maps from other sources (windows saved by route 3, MapBiomas at 10 m, state
maps, your own classifications) come in through a folder with one GeoTIFF per
year, named `prefix_year.tif`. `load_local_rasters()`:

1. checks each file: one layer, coordinate reference system, integer codes and
   coverage of the area;
2. harmonizes every year to the grid of the first with nearest neighbour, which
   does not mix class codes;
3. crops and masks by the area and handles no-data pixels (`nodata`, 0 by
   default).

The area can be in the folder itself. Maps that cover only part of the area,
such as windows saved for another region, are refused:

```{r eval=FALSE}
maps_again <- load_local_rasters(folder = "maps-lagoa", collection = 10)
```

When the collection uses the MapBiomas legend, `collection = 10` brings names and
colours. For another legend, `class_dictionary()` builds a template with the codes
present and then reads the completed dictionary (code, name and colour, in
Portuguese or English):

```{r eval=FALSE}
template <- class_dictionary(maps_again)
write.csv(template, "legend.csv", row.names = FALSE)
dictionary <- class_dictionary(maps_again, file = "legend.csv")
maps_again <- load_local_rasters(folder = "maps-lagoa", dictionary = dictionary)
```

## Which route to use {-}

| | Selective download | National collection | HTTP reading | Local folder |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Collections | MapBiomas Brazil | MapBiomas Brazil | catalogue or URL | any |
| Transfer | the area's tiles | ~28 GB, once | only the area's window | none |
| Internet | on the first run | only to download | yes | no |
| Best for | a few areas | many areas, offline use | 10 m, other countries, few years | own and saved maps |

## Extended context {-}

Connectivity indices suffer from edge effects: the area boundary cuts fragments
and hides stepping stones outside it. `context_m` widens the reading with a band
around the area, in metres. The object keeps the original area as `focal`, used
by the connectivity analyses (chapter \@ref(lagoa-context)):

```{r eval=FALSE}
maps_context <- load_rasters(ufscar, start = 2024, end = 2024, method = "http",
                             product = "mapbiomas_brasil_c10", context_m = 2000)
```

## The maps object {-}

All four routes return a list with the area boundary (`shape`), the period
(`time_range`), one map per year (`raster`) and the collection (`collection`). It
also keeps the origin of the maps (`source`), which allows a larger area to be
reloaded through the same route; the class dictionary (`class_dictionary`), for
local collections; the original area (`focal`), with a context; and reading
details (`metadata`). The object can be saved and shared, so the acquisition does
not need to be repeated:

```{r eval=FALSE}
save(maps, file = "lagoa-do-sino.Rdata")
load("lagoa-do-sino.Rdata")
```

The package already includes the maps object for the Lagoa do Sino example area,
from 1985 to 2024, which is used throughout Part II.
